question: What first got you interested in electrical engineering?
lookingFor: A specific, personal moment of curiosity that turned into sustained interest, not a vague love of gadgets.

bullets: Name a concrete moment, project, or experience that sparked it
Show the interest has continued and deepened over time
Avoid generic claims like 'I've always loved technology'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I took apart an old radio when I was about twelve because it stopped working, and I got completely absorbed trying to figure out which component had failed. That curiosity turned into building small circuits with my dad's old multimeter, and by the time I got to sixth form I was choosing physics options specifically because they touched on electromagnetism. It's stayed consistent rather than being a passing phase, which is why I'm confident this is the right subject for me.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always liked gadgets' with no specific story
Describing an interest that sounds more like computer science or coding
Giving an answer with no timeline showing sustained interest
followUps: What have you done since then to keep exploring that interest?

subtopic: Why electrical over other engineering disciplines
question: Why electrical engineering rather than mechanical or civil engineering?
lookingFor: A clear-eyed comparison showing the applicant understands what distinguishes electrical engineering, not just a preference by elimination.

bullets: Identify what is genuinely distinct about electrical engineering as a discipline
Reference a specific experience that pointed toward electrical rather than the alternatives
Show respect for the other disciplines rather than dismissing them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked seriously at mechanical engineering too, since I enjoy building things, but what pulled me toward electrical was a school project on renewable energy where I had to design a small solar charge controller. I liked that the problem was invisible in a way mechanical systems aren't, you have to reason about voltage and current you can't directly see, and that abstraction appealed to me more than moving parts. I still respect mechanical engineering enormously, it just wasn't where my curiosity kept returning.

commonMistakes: Answering only by process of elimination with no positive reason
Showing a shaky grasp of what mechanical or civil engineering actually involves
Sounding dismissive of the other disciplines
followUps: Is there any overlap between electrical engineering and those fields that interests you?

question: Why do you want to study electrical engineering here specifically?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course structure, labs, or staff, connected to the applicant's own goals.

bullets: Name a specific course feature, lab, or module rather than generic praise
Connect that feature to a concrete personal interest or project
Show understanding of what sets this course apart from similar ones
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course lets students take a power systems specialisation from second year, which is unusual this early, and that matters to me because I spent last summer volunteering with a group installing solar panels in a rural community and I want to go deeper into grid integration. I also read about the microgrid testbed in your power lab, which is exactly the kind of hands-on facility I haven't had access to before. It felt like the course was built for someone who already knows which direction they want to specialise in.

commonMistakes: Praise that would apply equally to any university's engineering course
Citing rankings or reputation instead of course content
Naming a facility or module that doesn't actually exist in the course
followUps: What would you want to specialise in if you had a free choice in your final year?

question: Tell us about a project or hobby where you've applied electrical engineering ideas.
lookingFor: A genuine, specific project that shows practical engagement, including what went wrong and how it was fixed.

bullets: Describe a specific build with enough technical detail to show real involvement
Mention a problem encountered and how it was diagnosed or solved
Explain what was learned, not just what was completed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I built a simple line-following robot using an Arduino, an H-bridge motor driver, and two infrared sensors. The first version kept overshooting the line because I hadn't accounted for motor response lag, so I ended up reading about proportional control and adding a basic feedback loop that scaled motor speed to how far off the line the sensors read. It was the first time I really understood feedback control as more than a textbook diagram, because I had to debug it by watching the robot fail repeatedly.

commonMistakes: Describing a project too vaguely to prove real involvement
Claiming full credit for a heavily guided kit or school assignment
Skipping over any problems, making it sound suspiciously smooth
followUps: What would you change if you built it again?

question: What have you read or watched recently that relates to electrical engineering, and what did you take from it?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine intellectual engagement beyond the syllabus, with a considered personal reaction rather than a summary.

bullets: Name a specific, credible source rather than something vague
Summarise the core idea briefly rather than at length
Give a personal opinion or connection to their own thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read an IEEE Spectrum article on gallium nitride power transistors replacing silicon in chargers and power supplies. What struck me was how a materials change at the semiconductor level can ripple all the way through to smaller, cooler consumer electronics, which I hadn't really connected before. It made me want to understand semiconductor physics properly rather than just treating transistors as black-box switches, which is part of why I'm drawn to a course with a strong device physics component.

commonMistakes: Naming a source but being unable to explain its actual content
Choosing something too basic or too far outside electrical engineering
Summarising with no personal reaction or opinion
followUps: Did the article raise any questions you'd want to investigate further?

question: Can you explain Ohm's law and how you'd use it to find the current in a simple circuit?
lookingFor: A clear statement of V = IR with correct reasoning about how the quantities relate, applied to a concrete example.

bullets: State the relationship correctly: voltage equals current times resistance
Explain what each quantity physically represents
Walk through applying it to find an unknown value in a simple example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Ohm's law says voltage equals current multiplied by resistance, so V equals I times R. Voltage is the push driving charge round the circuit, resistance is how much the material opposes that flow, and current is the resulting rate of charge flow. So if I have a nine volt battery connected to a three ohm resistor, I can rearrange to get current equals voltage over resistance, which gives three amps. It's the relationship I reach for first whenever I'm trying to sanity check any circuit.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which variable is which in the formula
Stating the formula without being able to apply it to numbers
Confusing resistance with power
followUps: How does that change if you add a second resistor in series?

question: What's the difference between alternating current and direct current, and why do we use AC for mains power?
lookingFor: Correct technical distinction plus a practical reason grounded in transmission efficiency, not just a memorised fact.

bullets: Explain that DC flows in one direction while AC periodically reverses
Connect AC to the ability to transform voltage levels efficiently
Link that to reduced transmission losses over long distances
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Direct current flows steadily in one direction, like from a battery, while alternating current reverses direction periodically, usually as a sine wave at fifty or sixty hertz. We use AC for mains power mainly because transformers let us step voltage up and down easily, and stepping voltage up for transmission means less current for the same power, which cuts resistive losses in the cables. DC transmission exists too for very long distance links, but AC's ease of transformation is what made it the historical winner for the grid.

commonMistakes: Only describing the waveform shape with no mention of why AC won historically
Confusing frequency with voltage
Claiming DC can't be transformed at all rather than explaining it's harder
followUps: Where do you still see DC being used despite AC dominating the grid?

question: What does a capacitor do in a circuit, and how does it behave differently to a resistor?
lookingFor: Correct physical understanding of charge storage and the time-dependent, frequency-dependent behaviour compared to a resistor's fixed opposition.

bullets: Explain that a capacitor stores energy in an electric field between plates
Note that its opposition to current depends on frequency, unlike a resistor's fixed resistance
Give a practical use such as smoothing or filtering
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A capacitor stores energy by building up charge on two plates separated by an insulator, rather than dissipating energy as heat the way a resistor does. Its opposition to current, its impedance, isn't fixed like resistance, it depends on frequency, so it blocks DC once charged but lets higher frequency AC signals through more easily. That's why you see capacitors used for smoothing out ripples in a power supply, they charge and discharge to fill in the gaps left by rectified AC.

commonMistakes: Describing a capacitor as if it behaves exactly like a resistor
Forgetting that a fully charged capacitor blocks steady DC current
Giving no real-world application
followUps: What happens to a capacitor's impedance as frequency increases?

question: How does an inductor store energy, and why does it resist sudden changes in current?
lookingFor: Understanding that inductors store energy in a magnetic field and that induced EMF opposes rapid current change, tied to Lenz's law.

bullets: Explain energy storage in the magnetic field of a coil
Connect resistance to sudden current change to induced back EMF
Reference Lenz's law or the underlying physical principle
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field that builds up around a coil of wire as current flows through it. If you try to change that current quickly, the changing magnetic field induces a voltage that opposes the change, which is essentially Lenz's law in action, the induced EMF always fights whatever caused it. That's why inductors resist sudden current changes and why you get a voltage spike if you abruptly break a circuit with an inductive load, which is something you have to design around in switching circuits.

commonMistakes: Confusing inductors with capacitors and their storage mechanism
Stating the effect without any physical reasoning
Omitting the practical consequence, like voltage spikes on sudden switching
followUps: Where have you seen this cause a practical problem, like arcing at a switch?

question: What do Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws state, and why are they useful?
lookingFor: Accurate statement of both laws with an intuitive grasp of the conservation principles behind them.

bullets: State the current law: current into a node equals current out
State the voltage law: voltages around any closed loop sum to zero
Connect both to conservation of charge and energy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Kirchhoff's current law says the total current flowing into a junction has to equal the total flowing out, which is really just conservation of charge, current can't pile up or vanish at a node. Kirchhoff's voltage law says that if you go around any closed loop in a circuit, the sum of the voltage rises and drops has to be zero, which reflects conservation of energy. Together they're the backbone of solving more complicated circuits with multiple loops and branches, because they give you enough equations to find every unknown current and voltage.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which law applies to current and which to voltage
Stating the laws without any physical justification
Not being able to explain why they're useful for analysis
followUps: How would you use these laws to analyse a circuit with two loops?

question: How does a diode work, and why does it only conduct in one direction?
lookingFor: Basic but accurate grasp of the p-n junction and depletion region, connected to the practical one-way conduction behaviour.

bullets: Reference the p-n junction and the depletion region it creates
Explain forward bias shrinking the depletion region to allow current flow
Explain reverse bias widening it and blocking current
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A diode is built from a junction between p-type and n-type semiconductor material, and where they meet, a depletion region forms with no free charge carriers, which normally blocks current. When you forward bias it, applying positive voltage to the p-side, that depletion region shrinks and eventually current flows freely once you're past the material's threshold voltage. In reverse bias the depletion region widens instead, so almost no current flows, which is why the diode acts as a one-way valve for current.

commonMistakes: Describing the diode purely as a black box that 'lets current through one way'
Confusing forward and reverse bias
Not mentioning the depletion region at all
followUps: What happens to a diode if you exceed its reverse breakdown voltage?

question: In simple terms, how can a transistor act as both a switch and an amplifier?
lookingFor: Understanding that a small control signal governs a larger current, applied differently depending on operating region.

bullets: Explain that a small base or gate signal controls a much larger current
Distinguish switching, driving the transistor fully on or off, from amplification, keeping it in the linear region
Give a simple practical example of each use
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A transistor lets a small current or voltage at the base or gate control a much larger current flowing between the other two terminals. If you drive it hard between fully on and fully off, it behaves like a switch, which is how digital logic gates and power control circuits work. If instead you keep it in between, in its linear region, small changes in the input signal produce proportionally larger changes in the output current, which is how it amplifies a weak signal, like in an audio preamp.

commonMistakes: Only describing the switching use and forgetting amplification, or vice versa
Confusing which terminal controls which in a BJT or MOSFET
Giving no concrete example of either application
followUps: What determines whether a transistor is operating in its linear region rather than as a switch?

question: What is an op-amp, and what are the two golden rules you'd use to analyse one in a feedback circuit?
lookingFor: Familiarity with the idealised op-amp model and confidence applying the standard analysis shortcuts.

bullets: Describe an op-amp as a high-gain differential amplifier
State the two golden rules: no current into the inputs, and the inputs are at equal voltage under negative feedback
Mention a simple configuration, like an inverting or non-inverting amplifier
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An op-amp is a high gain differential amplifier, it amplifies the difference between its two input terminals by an enormous factor. When it's used with negative feedback, you can analyse it using two golden rules, no current flows into either input terminal, and the two input terminals sit at essentially the same voltage. Using those two rules on something like an inverting amplifier lets you derive the gain just from the ratio of the feedback and input resistors, without needing to know the op-amp's actual internal gain.

commonMistakes: Describing an op-amp as if it just passes the input through unchanged
Forgetting the golden rules only hold under negative feedback
Being unable to connect the rules to an actual circuit example
followUps: How would the golden rules change if the op-amp were in positive feedback instead?

question: What is power factor, and why does a low power factor matter to a utility company?
lookingFor: Understanding of real versus apparent power and the practical, economic consequence of a poor power factor.

bullets: Define power factor as the ratio of real power to apparent power
Explain that it arises from phase difference between voltage and current in reactive loads
Connect a low power factor to higher current for the same useful power, and the resulting infrastructure cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Power factor is the ratio of real power, the power actually doing useful work, to apparent power, which is just voltage times current. It drops below one whenever there's a phase difference between voltage and current, which happens with inductive loads like motors. A low power factor matters to utilities because it means more current has to flow to deliver the same real power, which increases losses in cables and transformers, so many industrial customers get penalised on their bill if their power factor is too low without correction.

commonMistakes: Defining power factor only as a number with no physical meaning
Confusing real power with apparent power
Not connecting it to any practical or economic consequence
followUps: How would you go about correcting a poor power factor in an industrial plant?

question: How does a transformer step voltage up or down, and why does it only work with AC?
lookingFor: Correct grasp of mutual induction between windings and why a changing flux is required, ruling out steady DC.

bullets: Explain mutual induction between primary and secondary windings via a shared magnetic core
Reference the turns ratio determining the voltage ratio
Explain why a steady DC current produces no changing flux and therefore no induced voltage
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A transformer has two coils wound around a shared magnetic core, and a changing current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic flux that induces a voltage in the secondary coil. The ratio of turns between the two coils sets the ratio between primary and secondary voltage, so more turns on the secondary steps voltage up. It only works with AC because the induction depends on the flux actually changing over time, a steady DC current produces a constant flux with no rate of change, so nothing gets induced in the secondary.

commonMistakes: Explaining transformers as if they work through direct electrical connection between windings
Forgetting to mention the turns ratio
Being unable to explain why DC doesn't work
followUps: What happens to current when voltage is stepped up, and why does that matter for efficiency?

question: What's the difference between an analog and a digital signal, and why might you convert one to the other?
lookingFor: Clear distinction between continuous and discrete representation, plus a practical reason for conversion such as noise resilience.

bullets: Explain analog as continuously varying and digital as discrete levels
Give a reason for converting, such as noise immunity or ease of processing and storage
Mention where conversion actually happens, like an ADC
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An analog signal varies continuously and can take any value within a range, like the voltage from a microphone. A digital signal instead represents information as discrete levels, usually binary, sampled at set intervals. We convert analog to digital using an analog to digital converter, mainly because digital signals are far more resistant to noise and much easier to process, store, and transmit accurately with modern computing hardware, even though we lose some information through sampling and quantisation.

commonMistakes: Saying digital signals are simply 'more accurate' with no real explanation
Confusing analog with just being 'old technology'
Not mentioning the trade-off of information loss through sampling
followUps: What determines how much information you lose when sampling an analog signal?

subtopic: Interest in renewable energy and grid
question: What do you see as the biggest electrical engineering challenge in integrating renewable energy into the grid?
lookingFor: An informed, specific technical challenge rather than a vague sustainability sentiment, showing genuine engagement with the field.

bullets: Identify a specific technical challenge, such as intermittency or grid stability
Explain why it's genuinely difficult from an engineering standpoint
Show awareness of at least one approach being used to address it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the hardest part is intermittency and how it affects grid stability, wind and solar output doesn't match demand the way a dispatchable gas or coal plant does, and the grid needs constant frequency and voltage regulation to stay stable. That's a real engineering problem, not just a policy one, because inverter-based generation doesn't naturally provide the rotational inertia that traditional generators gave the grid for free. I've been reading about grid-forming inverters as one way to synthesise that stability, which is the kind of control problem I'd love to work on.

commonMistakes: Staying at the level of 'renewables are good for the planet' with no engineering substance
Naming a challenge but being unable to explain why it's hard
Confusing generation technology with grid infrastructure issues
followUps: How does energy storage help address that challenge?

question: Can you explain Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and give an everyday example of it in action?
lookingFor: Correct statement of the relationship between changing flux and induced EMF, with a genuine real-world application.

bullets: State that a changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an EMF
Note that the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of flux
Give a real example such as a generator, induction hob, or wireless charger
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Faraday's law says that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force in that circuit, and the size of that EMF is proportional to how fast the flux is changing. It's the principle behind a generator, spinning a coil in a magnetic field constantly changes the flux through it and induces a voltage, which is how mechanical energy gets converted into electrical energy. I also think about it every time I use a wireless phone charger, since that's really just induction between two coils without any physical contact.

commonMistakes: Stating the law without connecting flux change to the induced voltage
Confusing Faraday's law with Ohm's law
Giving no real-world example, or an incorrect one
followUps: What does Lenz's law add to this picture?

question: What is negative feedback in a control system, and why is it generally preferred over open-loop control?
lookingFor: Solid conceptual grasp of closed-loop correction and its advantages over uncorrected open-loop operation, with awareness of trade-offs.

bullets: Explain that negative feedback compares output to a desired reference and corrects the error
Contrast this with open-loop control, which has no way to correct for disturbances
Show awareness that feedback introduces its own challenges, like potential instability
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Negative feedback means you measure the actual output, compare it against the desired reference, and feed the difference, the error, back into the system to correct it, like a thermostat adjusting heating based on measured room temperature. Open-loop control has no such correction, it just applies a fixed input and hopes the result matches expectations, which fails badly if there are disturbances or the system's behaviour isn't perfectly known. The trade-off is that feedback systems can become unstable if the gain and delays aren't tuned properly, so designing a good controller means balancing responsiveness against the risk of oscillation.

commonMistakes: Describing feedback vaguely as 'checking the output' with no mention of error correction
Failing to name a concrete real-world example
Missing the trade-off around stability entirely
followUps: What could cause a feedback system to become unstable?

question: In simple terms, what does it mean to look at a signal in the frequency domain rather than the time domain, and why is that useful?
lookingFor: An intuitive, correct explanation of decomposing a signal into frequency components, with a practical reason for doing so.

bullets: Explain that any signal can be thought of as a sum of sine waves at different frequencies
Contrast time domain, showing value over time, with frequency domain, showing which frequencies are present
Give a practical reason it's useful, such as filtering or identifying noise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In the time domain you're looking at how a signal's value changes moment to moment, but almost any signal can also be described as a combination of simple sine waves added together at different frequencies and amplitudes, which is what the frequency domain shows you. It's useful because some problems are much clearer that way, if you want to remove a specific hum or noise frequency from an audio signal, it's far easier to spot and filter it out when you can see exactly which frequency it sits at, rather than trying to see it buried in a messy time-domain waveform.

commonMistakes: Reciting 'Fourier transform' with no intuitive explanation of what it does
Confusing frequency domain with just 'pitch' in an overly narrow, audio-only sense
Giving no practical reason why the frequency view is useful
followUps: Can you think of an everyday device that relies on this idea?

question: What do you think is the biggest challenge facing electrical engineers over the next decade?
lookingFor: An informed, well-reasoned opinion on a genuine industry challenge, showing awareness of engineering trade-offs rather than headlines alone.

bullets: Pick a real, specific challenge rather than something too broad or vague
Explain the engineering dimension of the problem, not just the social or economic angle
Offer a considered, even if tentative, view on how it might be addressed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd say it's decarbonising the electricity grid while keeping it reliable, because electrifying transport and heating is going to roughly double electricity demand in a lot of countries at the same time we're retiring dispatchable fossil generation. That's a genuinely hard control and infrastructure problem, not just a policy target, since you need enough storage, flexible demand, and smarter grid control to keep supply and demand balanced without the inertia that old spinning generators used to provide for free. I don't think there's one clean answer yet, which is honestly part of why I find it so compelling to want to work on.

commonMistakes: Naming a challenge that's really a general societal issue with no engineering content
Reciting a headline with no personal reasoning behind it
Claiming to have a complete, confident solution to a genuinely unresolved problem
followUps: What role do you think you personally could play in addressing that?

subtopic: Ethics and safety in electrical design
question: Imagine you're testing a circuit design and notice it technically passes the safety spec but you're uneasy about a corner case. What would you do?
lookingFor: Sound ethical reasoning that prioritises genuine safety over minimum compliance, with a realistic account of how to raise the concern.

bullets: Recognise that passing a spec is not the same as being genuinely safe
Describe a concrete step, like documenting the concern and raising it with a supervisor or mentor
Show they wouldn't just quietly let it go, nor act unilaterally without more investigation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Passing a spec on paper doesn't mean the design is actually safe in every situation, specs are usually written for common cases and can miss edge conditions, so I wouldn't just wave it through. I'd document exactly what the corner case is and why it worries me, then raise it clearly with whoever is supervising the project rather than either staying silent or trying to unilaterally redesign it myself. Electrical faults can genuinely hurt people, so I'd rather be the person who over-communicates a concern than the one who assumed someone else would catch it.

commonMistakes: Saying they'd simply ignore it because it technically passes
Jumping to drastic unilateral action without raising it through proper channels
Treating the question as purely hypothetical with no concrete plan
followUps: What would you do if your supervisor dismissed your concern?

subtopic: Role of programming in electrical engineering
question: How important do you think programming is for an electrical engineer, and where have you used it yourself?
lookingFor: Realistic understanding of where software meets hardware in the field, backed by genuine personal experience if any exists.

bullets: Explain where programming genuinely intersects with electrical engineering, such as embedded systems or simulation
Avoid overstating it as the whole discipline, since electrical engineering is broader than software
Give a specific, honest example of their own experience with it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think programming matters a lot in areas like embedded systems, control, and signal processing, where you're writing the code that actually runs on a microcontroller talking to real hardware, but I wouldn't say it's the whole of electrical engineering, plenty of power and analog design work is much more about physical circuit behaviour. I taught myself some C for an Arduino project where I had to write the code controlling motor speed based on sensor readings, and debugging timing issues between the code and the actual electrical signals was where I learned the two sides really do depend on each other.

commonMistakes: Claiming electrical engineering is essentially the same as software engineering
Dismissing programming as unimportant to the discipline
Giving a generic answer with no actual personal example
followUps: What's a bug you ran into where the problem turned out to be hardware, not code?

question: A lot of students interested in technology end up choosing computer science. Why did you choose electrical engineering instead?
lookingFor: A thoughtful comparison showing the applicant actually weighed the alternative, not a reflexive dismissal of computer science.

bullets: Acknowledge computer science as a genuine alternative they considered seriously
Identify what specifically pulls them toward the physical and electrical side rather than pure software
Ground the choice in a concrete experience rather than an abstract preference
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I actually considered computer science quite seriously, since I enjoy coding, but what I kept missing in pure software projects was the physical layer, actually reasoning about voltage, current, and real components rather than working entirely in an abstraction. Building a small power supply for a school project made that clear, I liked the parts where I had to measure real signals with an oscilloscope and figure out why my theoretical calculations didn't quite match what I was seeing. Electrical engineering lets me keep the problem-solving I enjoy from coding while staying grounded in the physical world, which is the combination I actually want.

commonMistakes: Dismissing computer science as somehow lesser or 'not real engineering'
Giving an answer with no concrete grounding, just abstract preference
Sounding as if they haven't actually thought about the alternative
followUps: Is there a part of computer science you'd still want to bring into your electrical engineering work?

subtopic: A recent development that excites them
question: What recent development in electrical engineering do you find most exciting, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine, informed enthusiasm for a specific real development, with an understanding of why it matters technically, not just that it's trendy.

bullets: Name a specific, real, and reasonably current development
Explain the underlying technical reason it's significant, not just its popularity
Connect it honestly to their own interests or goals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following the shift toward wide-bandgap semiconductors like silicon carbide and gallium nitride in power electronics, because they can switch faster and handle higher voltages with less energy lost as heat than traditional silicon devices. That matters practically because it's making electric vehicle inverters and fast chargers smaller and more efficient, which is a real bottleneck in EV adoption right now. I find it exciting because it's a case where a fairly fundamental materials science change is having an immediate, visible impact on a technology I care about.

commonMistakes: Naming something too vague or buzzword-heavy, like 'AI' with no electrical engineering connection
Being unable to explain the technical reason it matters
Sounding like they read one headline with no deeper engagement
followUps: What do you see as the main obstacle to that technology becoming mainstream?
